content: 1. Antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended for pregnant women to prevent recurrent urinary tract infections (RUTI) only in the context of rigorous research. 2. Antenatal prophylaxis with anti-D immunoglobulin is recommended for non-sensitized Rh-negative pregnant women at 28 and 34 weeks of gestation to prevent RhD allo-immunization, but only in the context of rigorous research. 3. Preventive anthelmintic treatment is recommended for pregnant women in endemic areas after the first trimester as part of worm infection reduction programs. 4. Eligible pregnant women should be routinely immunized at their first contact with antenatal clinics or other health services offering vaccination. Women with inadequate or unknown immunization history should receive two doses of tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine, with the first dose administered as early as possible during pregnancy and the second dose at least four weeks later. 5. Pregnant women should be vaccinated with trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine at any stage of pregnancy. 6. In malaria-endemic areas, mothers and babies should sleep under insecticide-impregnated bed nets. 7. In malaria-endemic areas in Africa, intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) is recommended for all pregnant women, starting in the second trimester, with doses given at least one month apart to ensure at least three doses are received. 8. The G6PD status of patients should guide the administration of primaquine to prevent relapse in P. vivax or P. ovale malaria. When G6PD status is unknown and testing is unavailable, the decision to prescribe primaquine must be based on an assessment of risks and benefits. 9. Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) containing tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) should be offered as an additional prevention choice for pregnant women at substantial risk of HIV infection as part of combination prevention approaches. 10. Ginger, chamomile, vitamin B6, and/or acupuncture are recommended for relieving nausea in early pregnancy, based on a woman’s preferences and available options. 11. Advice on diet and lifestyle is recommended to prevent and relieve heartburn in pregnancy. Antacid preparations can be offered to women with troublesome symptoms not relieved by lifestyle modification. 12. Magnesium, calcium, or non-pharmacological treatment options can be used for relieving leg cramps in pregnancy, based on a woman’s preferences and available options. 13. Regular exercise throughout pregnancy is recommended to prevent low back and pelvic pain. Treatment options such as physiotherapy, support belts, and acupuncture can be used based on a woman’s preferences and available options. 14. Wheat bran or other fiber supplements can be used to relieve constipation in pregnancy if dietary modification fails, based on a woman’s preferences and available options. 15. Non-pharmacological options such as compression stockings, leg elevation, and water immersion can be used for managing varicose veins and edema in pregnancy, based on a woman’s preferences and available options. 16. Each pregnant woman should carry her own case notes during pregnancy to improve continuity, quality of care, and her pregnancy experience. 17. Midwife-led continuity-of-care models, where a known midwife or small group of midwives supports a woman throughout the antenatal, intrapartum, and postnatal continuum, are recommended in settings with well-functioning midwifery programs. 18. Group antenatal care provided by qualified healthcare professionals may be offered as an alternative to individual antenatal care in the context of rigorous research, depending on a woman’s preferences and the availability of infrastructure and resources. 19. Community mobilization through facilitated participatory learning and action (PLA) cycles with women’s groups is recommended to improve maternal and newborn health, particularly in rural settings with low access to health services. 20. Packages of interventions that include household and community mobilization and antenatal home visits are recommended to improve antenatal care utilization and perinatal health outcomes, particularly in rural settings with low access to health services. 21. Task shifting the promotion of health-related behaviors for maternal and newborn health to a broad range of cadres, including lay health workers, auxiliary nurses, nurses, midwives, and doctors, is recommended. 22. Task shifting the distribution of recommended nutritional supplements and intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) for malaria prevention to a broad range of cadres, including auxiliary nurses, nurses, midwives, and doctors, is recommended. 23. Policymakers should consider educational, regulatory, financial, and personal and professional support interventions to recruit and retain qualified health workers in rural and remote areas. 24. Antenatal care models with a minimum of eight contacts are recommended to reduce perinatal mortality and improve women’s experience of care. 25. Low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin, 75 mg) is recommended for the prevention of pre-eclampsia in women at high risk of developing the condition. It should be initiated before 20 weeks of pregnancy. 26. Women with severe hypertension during pregnancy should receive treatment with antihypertensive drugs. 27. Advice to rest at home is not recommended as an intervention for the primary prevention of pre-eclampsia and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in women at risk of developing these conditions. 28. Strict bed rest is not recommended for improving pregnancy outcomes in women with hypertension (with or without proteinuria) in pregnancy. 29. Restriction in dietary salt intake during pregnancy with the aim of preventing the development of pre-eclampsia and its complications is not recommended. 30. Diuretics, particularly thiazides, are not recommended for the prevention of pre-eclampsia and its complications. 31. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is recommended for women at risk of preterm birth from 24 to 34 weeks of gestation when specific conditions are met, including accurate gestational age assessment, imminent preterm birth, no clinical evidence of maternal infection, and availability of adequate childbirth and newborn care. 32. For eligible women, antenatal corticosteroids should be administered when preterm birth is considered imminent within seven days of starting treatment, including within the first 24 hours. 33. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is recommended for women at risk of preterm birth irrespective of whether a single or multiple birth is anticipated. 34. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is recommended in women with preterm prelabor rupture of membranes and no clinical signs of infection. 35. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is not recommended in women with chorioamnionitis who are likely to deliver preterm. 36. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is not recommended in women undergoing planned cesarean section at late preterm gestations (34–36+6 weeks). 37. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is recommended in women with hypertensive disorders in pregnancy who are at risk of imminent preterm birth. 38. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is recommended for women at risk of imminent preterm birth of a growth-restricted fetus. 39. Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is recommended for women with pre-gestational and gestational diabetes who are at risk of imminent preterm birth, accompanied by interventions to optimize maternal blood glucose control. 40. Either intramuscular (IM) dexamethasone or IM betamethasone (total 24 mg in divided doses) is recommended as the antenatal corticosteroid of choice when preterm birth is imminent. 41. A single repeat course of antenatal corticosteroid is recommended if preterm birth does not occur within seven days after the initial dose, and a subsequent clinical assessment demonstrates a high risk of preterm birth in the next seven days. 42. Tocolytic treatments (acute and maintenance treatments) are not recommended for women at risk of imminent preterm birth for the purpose of improving newborn outcomes. 43. The use of magnesium sulfate is recommended for women at risk of imminent preterm birth before 32 weeks of gestation for the prevention of cerebral palsy in the infant and child. 44. Routine antibiotic administration is not recommended for women in preterm labor with intact amniotic membranes and no clinical signs of infection. 45. Antibiotic administration is recommended for women with preterm prelabor rupture of membranes. 46. Erythromycin is recommended as the antibiotic of choice for prophylaxis in women with preterm prelabor rupture of membranes. 47. The use of a combination of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid (“co-amoxiclav”) is not recommended for women with preterm prelabor rupture of membranes. 48. Routine delivery by cesarean section for the purpose of improving preterm newborn outcomes is not recommended, regardless of cephalic or breech presentation.
